newsitem.title: USA: Rubin defends strong-dollar policy against attacks.
newsitem.headline: Rubin defends strong-dollar policy against attacks.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Monday that the Clinton administration has no plans to change its strong-dollar policy, despite stepped-up criticism from U.S. manufacturing companies.
"A strong dollar helps to keep interest rates down, helps to keep inflation down," he told Reuters in an interview. "It's very much in our interest."
U.S. manufacturers attacked the strong-dollar policy last week, saying the currency's steep rise versus the yen over the past 1-1/2 years is damaging U.S. exports and growth.

Rubin said he did not know whether Japan was manipulating the currency market to keep the yen down so as to improve the competitiveness of its exports -- a charge also made by the manufacturers. But he made clear that the Japanese stance should not alter the administration's position on the dollar:
"I don't know if they're using it as a trade tool. But I don't think what they're doing should affect what we do."

He said the Treasury has regular discussions with Japan's Ministry of Finance (MoF) on a range of issues, including currency rates, but declined to say whether the administration had or would call Tokyo to task for manipulating the yen.

"As to the question of whether we should call them to task, I think I'd limit my comment there to say we do have ... regular interchanges with the MoF where we discuss all the areas of mutual interest," Rubin said. "I don't want to get into the content of the conversations," he added.
As he has done before, Rubin argued that it was in Japan's best interests -- and that of the world -- that it have a strong economy led by domestic demand.
Rubin said Japan needed to be "watchful" about the course of its economy as it phases out the fiscal stimulus to its economy from higher spending and expanded tax breaks.

The Treasury chief said that European nations also needed to be "watchful" about the course of their economies as they move toward monetary union and should try to put in policies that promote solid growth with low inflation.
He played down worries that the introduction of the new European currency, the euro, in 1999 would undercut the dollar as the world's key reserve currency.
"I don't think there's a threat to the dollar," Rubin said, explaining that the market for dollar-denominated investments is very large and very deep.

"Ultimately, what the dollar does will be a function of policies that the government takes, the success of the private sector in being competitive and all the other conditions that contribute to a currency's behavior," he added.

European central banks are expected to be saddled with tens of billions of dollars in excess dollar reserves once the euro is launched, and some analysts have voiced concern they could be dumped on the market, undermining the greenback.
Rubin though said he believed that the excess dollars could be absorbed.
"Nobody knows exactly what those magnitudes are," he said. "Nobody seems particularly concerned about the ability to absorb them," he added.
